fact_text: The analyst argues a major geopolitical shock is largely priced into the market within the first one to two trading days, so later negative developments often add less than investors fear.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'PSX - War time Investing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: During an uncertain conflict, days with no new negative news let the market gradually price in a positive outlook, which the analyst frames as no news being good news.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'PSX - War time Investing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: A credible announcement of talks or of reopened economies can lift the market quickly even while sporadic attacks continue, because the market reacts to the direction of the news rather than to the attacks themselves.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'PSX - War time Investing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: If attacks continue every day and the market keeps halting, the analyst expects a much larger cumulative decline than the first-day reaction, because each day of escalation adds to the sell-off.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'PSX - War time Investing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst argues the US government has strong incentives to calm markets, because trillions of dollars of capital are exposed, and that US leadership has pushed for quick de-escalation when markets were under pressure.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'PSX - War time Investing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Attacks that shut regional airlines, tourism and oil supply chains create economic pressure on the parties to end hostilities, the analyst argues, even if the conflict is not fully resolved.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'PSX - War time Investing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The Strait of Hormuz is a key chokepoint for oil supply, so armed conflict and proxy attacks in that region can constrain global oil flows.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'PSX - War time Investing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Proxy attacks around the Strait of Hormuz can keep oil supply constrained even after a headline settlement, which the analyst treats as the main path to a prolonged oil shock.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'PSX - War time Investing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: If a supply route stays disrupted, buyers shift to alternative sources at a higher cost, which the analyst says turns a temporary oil spike into a structurally higher oil price.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'PSX - War time Investing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: In the analyst's prolonged-disruption scenario oil trades in roughly the 90 to 100 dollar range, a level he links to a slowdown in Pakistan's economy and its market.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'PSX - War time Investing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Higher oil prices widen Pakistan's oil import bill and push up inflation, two channels through which an oil shock weakens the economy and therefore the stock market.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'PSX - War time Investing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Oil-driven inflation can stop interest rates from falling or force a rate rise, and higher rates make the stock market less attractive relative to other asset classes.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'PSX - War time Investing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Oil futures trading that starts early in the session is a useful early signal for Pakistan market sentiment, since oil prices have a large impact on Pakistan.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'PSX - War time Investing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: Prolonged uncertainty keeps the market in negative territory, which creates persistent selling pressure for as long as the situation stays unresolved.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'PSX - War time Investing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst's conflict framework builds two plausible scenarios, uses a 72-hour window to watch for de-escalation, and sets a one-week checkpoint to decide which scenario is playing out.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'PSX - War time Investing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst warns that selling on the first day of a shock and planning to re-enter after a settlement locks in losses, since the price already reflects the expected negatives and re-entry comes after the rebound.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'PSX - War time Investing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst described staged entry during a shock: commit a small part of the capital on a sharp decline, add if the market falls further, and commit the rest only once de-escalation is confirmed.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'PSX - War time Investing' (YouTube transcript, undated)

fact_text: The analyst says no one can pinpoint the exact bottom; he judges an entry attractive when a specific company trades at a price he considers very undervalued, even while the index is still falling.
source_name: Abdul Rehman Najam, 'PSX - War time Investing' (YouTube transcript, undated)
